351.title: Mishpatim: the widow and the orphan (Exodus 22:21–23)
351.hook: God hears the cry of the widow and the fatherless
351.tomorrow: Mishpatim: we will do, and we will hear (Exodus 24:7)
351.howItsDone: Jewish communities have kept funds and societies for widows, orphans and the poor, and Jewish law, following Rashi and the Mekhilta, applies the ban on afflicting the widow and orphan to every person, with special care for the vulnerable.

segments.voice: Yesterday, in Mishpatim, the law of your enemy's fallen donkey. Your line was help your enemy's donkey. Today, the people with nobody to help them.

In an office there can be someone no one stands up for: the temp, the new hire with no friends yet, the cleaner who comes in after everyone's gone. If someone takes advantage of them, who will complain? Who will even notice? In the ancient world, the people in that position had names. A widow, with no husband to speak for her in court. An orphan, with no father to protect his inheritance. Easy people to cheat. The Torah turns to them directly, and does something unusual: it names who is listening.
screen: `THE ONE NOBODY STANDS UP FOR.` → `THE WIDOW AND THE ORPHAN.` → `WHO IS LISTENING?`

segments.voice: Here's the law, in the old Jewish translation: "Ye shall not afflict any widow, or fatherless child." Then: if you afflict them, and they cry out to me, I will surely hear their cry. In Hebrew, three verbs in that line are doubled. Afflict, you afflict. Cry, they cry. Hear, I will hear. It's the Hebrew way of saying: really, surely, I mean it. The next verse is fierce. It warns that the one who harms them will meet the same fate, their own wives widowed, their own children fatherless. Measure for measure. The Torah doesn't soften it, and this lesson won't either. Rashi asks a fair question. Is it only widows and orphans you mustn't afflict? No, he says, following the Mekhilta: the same law covers every person. The Torah names these two because they're the weakest and the easiest to hurt. The law speaks where the danger is greatest. Who has no protection now? A tenant without a lease. An elderly person living alone. A child in foster care. A worker far from home. The categories change; the shape doesn't. And notice where the verse puts God: not on the side of the powerful, the judge or the landowner, but at the ear of the person crying. Isaiah picks this up, telling Israel to judge the fatherless and plead for the widow.

segments.voice: Let one person around you who has nobody to speak for them come into focus: an older neighbor living alone, a new coworker, a kid at the edge of the playground. What do they need that they can't ask for? If you pray, you can hold them before God, who the verse says surely hears; if not, simply listen, the way you'd want someone to listen to you.
Mishpatim. The ordinances. Today, the law that protects the widow and the fatherless, and says God surely hears their cry.
Your line: God hears them. The quietest cry is the one the verse names. See you tomorrow.

352.title: Mishpatim: we will do, and we will hear (Exodus 24:7)
352.hook: the people promise to act before they fully understand
352.howItsDone: Na'aseh v'nishma is a phrase Jewish teachers return to when speaking about commitment, often cited to encourage people to begin a practice, like lighting Shabbat candles or saying a blessing, and let understanding grow from doing it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the widow and the orphan, and the promise that their cry is heard. Your line was God hears them. Today, the last day of Mishpatim, and the people's answer.

Nobody learns to swim by reading about it. You can study the strokes, watch the videos, memorize when to breathe. None of it makes sense until you're in the water, swallowing some of the pool, and suddenly your body understands what the book was saying. Moses has written down the laws of the covenant. He reads them aloud to the whole people at the foot of the mountain. And they answer with two Hebrew words, in an order the rabbis would later dwell on.
screen: `NOBODY LEARNS TO SWIM BY READING.` → `SOME THINGS MAKE SENSE INSIDE.` → `THE PEOPLE ANSWER.`

segments.voice: Here's their answer, in the old Jewish translation: "All that the LORD hath spoken will we do, and obey." In Hebrew the last words are na'aseh v'nishma. Na'aseh: we will do. V'nishma: and we will hear. Obey is one meaning of the word, but nishma also means hear, listen, understand; it's the same root as the Shema: hear, O Israel. So the people say: we will do, and then we will understand. The Talmud tells a story about it. When Israel put we will do before we will hear, six hundred thousand angels came down and tied two crowns on each person, one for doing and one for hearing. A heavenly voice asked: who revealed to my children the secret the angels use? Because angels, a psalm says, do God's word first and hear afterward. The Talmud also records a skeptic mocking a rabbi: you impetuous people, putting your mouths before your ears! The rabbi answered that people who walk in trust can afford to. Reasonable people can disagree here, and Jewish tradition prizes asking questions too. The order doesn't mean don't think. It means some kinds of knowing only come by doing. Light the candles before you understand Shabbat. Sit with the mourners before you understand grief. And with that, Mishpatim ends: the details, the stranger, the enemy's donkey, the widow and orphan, and a people who said, we'll do it, and we'll learn.

segments.voice: Think of a practice you've been curious about but keep putting off until you understand it better: lighting candles on Friday night, a blessing before eating, a morning gratitude, a weekly walk in silence. Na'aseh v'nishma. We will do, and we will hear. The people's answer at Sinai, putting the doing before the understanding.
Your line: do, then understand. Some things only make sense from the inside. That's day three hundred fifty-two.

353.title: Terumah: willing hearts (Exodus 25:2)
353.hook: the sanctuary is built only from gifts "of every man whose heart maketh him willing"
353.howItsDone: In Jewish life, giving is both a duty and a gift: tzedakah is expected of everyone, and alongside it Jews also give freely to synagogues and causes, often recalling that the sanctuary was built from gifts of willing hearts.

segments.voice: Yesterday Mishpatim ended with na'aseh v'nishma, we will do and we will hear. Your line was do, then understand. Today, a new portion, and a building project.

Two gifts arrive in the same week. One is a gift card from a relative who was reminded to send something, with a printed signature. The other is a mug from a child, lopsided, thick with paint and glue, handed over with both hands. One cost more. Only one was made because someone wanted to make it. God is about to ask the people to build a sanctuary in the wilderness, a dwelling place for the divine presence. It will need gold, silver, fabric, wood, oil. And the very first instruction is about where all of it is allowed to come from.
screen: `A GIFT CARD, A LOPSIDED MUG.` → `WHICH ONE DO YOU KEEP?` → `A SANCTUARY, AND WHERE IT COMES FROM.`

segments.voice: The portion is called Terumah, and it begins, in the old Jewish translation: "Speak unto the children of Israel, that they take for Me an offering; of every man whose heart maketh him willing ye shall take My offering." Terumah is the Hebrew word for that offering. Its root means to lift up, to raise: something you lift out of what you have and set apart, the way you might lift the best piece onto someone else's plate. Then the list: gold, silver and copper; blue, purple and scarlet wool; fine linen and goats' hair; rams' skins dyed red; acacia wood; oil for the light; spices for the anointing oil and incense; onyx and other stones. But notice the condition. Not a tax. Not a quota. Only from every person whose heart moves them; the Hebrew is literally whose heart makes him willing, or urges him on. Readers have noticed something else in the first line. It says take for me an offering, not give. Some Hasidic teachers liked to say that when you give from the heart, you're also taking: you receive something by giving. Whether or not you read it that way, the point of the opening is plain. A house for God built from forced gifts wouldn't be the house the Torah has in mind. It has to start with willing hearts.

segments.voice: Set aside what you should give, or what's expected, and ask what you'd actually like to lift out of your life and offer: some time, a skill, an object someone else would love, a compliment you've been holding back. Let something come up that feels light to give, not heavy, and notice the difference between should and want to.
Terumah. An offering, something lifted up and set apart. The name of the portion where the sanctuary is built only from willing hearts.

354.title: Terumah: among them (Exodus 25:8)
354.hook: "that I may dwell among them", not in it; teachers read it as within each person
354.howItsDone: Many Jewish teachers read Exodus 25:8 as saying God dwells within each person, and the synagogue has long been called a mikdash me'at, a small sanctuary; many Jews also set aside a quiet corner at home for prayer or study.

segments.voice: Yesterday, terumah, the offering lifted from willing hearts. Your line was only what's willing. Today, still in Terumah, the reason for the whole building.

People who build a house often say the same thing a year later: the house was never really the point. The point was the dinners, the kids' height marks on the doorframe, the friends on the couch at midnight. The walls just made room for it. The Torah is about to spend chapter after chapter on a building: measurements in cubits, gold rings, wooden boards, curtains of blue and purple. Before any of that, one verse explains why. And there's a tiny word in it, one Hebrew suffix, that readers have been unpacking for centuries.
screen: `THE HOUSE WAS NEVER THE POINT.` → `CHAPTERS OF MEASUREMENTS.` → `ONE VERSE SAYS WHY.`

segments.voice: Here it is, in the old Jewish translation: "And let them make Me a sanctuary, that I may dwell among them." The Hebrew for dwell is shachan, the root of mishkan, the name for this portable sanctuary, the tabernacle, and of a later word, Shechinah, the indwelling presence of God. Now the tiny word. The verse doesn't say that I may dwell in it, in the building. It says b'tocham, among them, in their midst. Grammatically that's natural: God's presence will be in the middle of the camp. But many Jewish teachers, from the sixteenth century onward, read it more personally. B'tocham can also mean within them. Make me a sanctuary, they read, and I will dwell within each one of them. The building is a means; the people are the dwelling. Several commentators give this reading, and it became a favorite in Hasidic teaching. It doesn't erase the building: the Torah really does want the tabernacle built, in exact detail. It just shows where the details are pointing. That idea mattered enormously later. When the Temple in Jerusalem was destroyed, Jews kept praying, studying and gathering, in homes, in synagogues, anywhere. The sages called the synagogue a small sanctuary, borrowing a phrase from the prophet Ezekiel. A presence that dwells among people can travel wherever people go.

segments.voice: Look around for one small spot you could make quiet: a corner, a chair by a window, the car before you go in, or just this minute with your eyes closed. No gold or blue curtains needed, only a little space set apart. Sit in it now, and if you pray, invite the presence the verse speaks of; if not, notice what it's like to be still, here, inside yourself.
Terumah. Our portion of offerings and building plans, and its heart: make me a sanctuary, that I may dwell among them.
Your line: among them, not in it. The walls were only ever there to make room. Until tomorrow.

355.title: Terumah: gold inside and out (Exodus 25:11)
355.hook: the ark is gilded inside and out; the Talmud says a scholar's inside must match his outside (Yoma 72b)
355.tomorrow: Terumah: the cherubim face each other (Exodus 25:20–22)
355.howItsDone: Tocho k'baro, inside like outside, is a phrase in Jewish ethical teaching about integrity, and the ark's gold within and without is cited for it in sermons on Terumah.

segments.voice: Yesterday, in Terumah: make me a sanctuary, that I may dwell among them. Your line was among them, not in it. Today, the first object in the plans: the ark.

Some kitchens have a drawer like this. The front of it is lovely: painted wood, a brass handle. Pull it open and it's chaos: rubber bands, dead batteries, a key nobody can identify. People can be a bit like that drawer, a polished outside and a different story inside. The first thing the Torah describes in the sanctuary plans isn't a wall or an altar. It's a box: the ark that will hold the tablets of the covenant. And the instructions for gilding it are oddly specific about the inside.
screen: `A LOVELY DRAWER, CHAOS INSIDE.` → `THE FIRST OBJECT: A BOX.` → `GILDED WHERE NO ONE LOOKS.`

segments.voice: The ark is made of acacia wood, two and a half cubits long. Then the instruction, in the old Jewish translation: "within and without shalt thou overlay it." Gold on the outside, which people might glimpse. Gold on the inside, which almost no one would ever see. The tablets would sit in there, and the ark would stand in the holiest room, where, tradition says, only the high priest entered, once a year. So why gild the inside? The Talmud gives a picture. Betzalel, the craftsman, made three boxes, it says: a gold one, a wooden one, and another gold one. The wooden box sat inside the outer gold, and the inner gold sat inside the wood. Gold, wood, gold. Then Rava, a sage of Babylonia, draws the lesson: any scholar whose inside is not like his outside is not a true scholar. In Hebrew, tocho k'baro, his inside like his outside. Elsewhere the Talmud remembers Rabban Gamliel, head of the academy, who barred from the study hall any student whose inside did not match his outside. Notice the ark isn't solid gold. There's wood in the middle: ordinary, living material. Nobody is asked to be pure metal all the way through. The ask is simpler, and harder: be the same inside as you appear outside. Don't polish only the side people see.

segments.voice: Notice one place where your outside and inside don't match right now: calm at work and frayed underneath, generous on the surface and resentful inside, saying you're fine. Don't judge the gap; just see it honestly. Then ask what one small step toward matching might be, a true word to one person, or quiet inside work no one will see.
Terumah. Our portion, where the ark is overlaid with gold inside and out, and the Talmud says a scholar's inside must match the outside.
Your line: gold inside and out. Wood in the middle is allowed. See you tomorrow.

356.title: Terumah: the cherubim face each other (Exodus 25:20–22)
356.hook: two golden figures face one another, and God speaks from between them
356.howItsDone: The cherubim are studied in Terumah each year, and the synagogue ark takes its name from the sanctuary's ark; some Jewish teachers use the facing cherubim to speak about presence in marriage, friendship and study partners.

segments.voice: Yesterday the ark was gilded inside and out. Your line was gold inside and out. Today, what stands on top of the ark.

Two people sit at a café table, both on their phones. Shoulders angled away, eyes down, the occasional mm-hm. A minute later the phones go away. They turn toward each other, elbows on the table, and one of them says something true, and the other hears it. Same table. Different room entirely. On top of the ark, the Torah asks for a lid of pure gold, and on it two golden figures. The instructions say exactly which way they should face. And then God says where the voice will come from.
screen: `TWO PEOPLE, TWO PHONES.` → `THEN THEY TURN TOWARD EACH OTHER.` → `TWO GOLDEN FIGURES.`

segments.voice: The figures are called keruvim, cherubim. Forget the chubby baby angels of Renaissance paintings; that picture came much later. In the Torah, keruvim are winged guardians; in Genesis, keruvim guard the way back to the garden of Eden. Here, two of them are hammered out of the same piece of gold as the lid of the ark, one at each end. Their wings spread upward, sheltering the lid, and the old Jewish translation says they stand "with their faces one to another." Then God tells Moses: there I will meet with thee, and speak with thee, "from between the two cherubim." Not from the gold. Not from either figure. From the space between two faces turned toward each other. The Talmud has an odd and lovely detail. One sage says keruv sounds like the Aramaic for like a child, and so the cherubim had young faces. And it notices a problem. In the book of Chronicles, the cherubim in Solomon's Temple face the house, not each other. Which is it? The Talmud answers: when Israel does God's will, they face each other; when not, they turn away. The faces show the state of the relationship. Read mystically or not, the picture holds. Something holy can happen in the space between two people who are really facing one another. That space is where this text says the voice comes from.
screen: `KERUVIM: WINGED GUARDIANS.` · `FACES ONE TO ANOTHER.` · `FROM BETWEEN THE TWO CHERUBIM.` · `FACING, OR TURNED AWAY.` · then, large: `THE VOICE BETWEEN THE FACES.`

segments.voice: Picture a conversation you'll have today, with a partner, a child, a coworker, a friend, the way it usually goes: half-turned, glancing at a screen, thinking about the next thing. Now picture it again with your whole face toward them, phone down, eyes up, listening to the end of the sentence, and notice what changes in the space between you.
Keruvim. Cherubim. The two golden figures on the ark, facing each other, with the voice speaking from between them.
Your line: the voice between the faces. Holiness can live in a conversation. Day three hundred fifty-six, done.

357.title: Terumah: the poles stay in (Exodus 25:15)
357.hook: the ark's carrying poles are never removed, always ready to travel
357.howItsDone: Jewish tradition counts the ban on removing the ark's poles among the Torah's commandments, and teachers often read it as a sign that Torah study and practice travel with Jews wherever they live.

segments.voice: Yesterday, keruvim, the cherubim facing each other on the ark. Your line was the voice between the faces. Today, the last day of Terumah, and a small detail on the side of the ark.

Some people keep a go-bag by the door: a change of clothes, a phone charger, copies of important papers. Firefighters leave their boots standing inside their pants, ready to step into. New parents keep a hospital bag packed for weeks. Not because they expect to leave this minute, but because life moves, and they want to be ready when it does. The ark has rings on its sides, two on each side, and through them, two wooden poles covered in gold. Most furniture loses its handles once it's in place. Not this.
screen: `A GO-BAG BY THE DOOR.` → `BOOTS READY TO STEP INTO.` → `RINGS AND POLES ON THE ARK.`

segments.voice: The instruction, in the old Jewish translation: "The staves shall be in the rings of the ark; they shall not be taken from it." Staves means the carrying poles, in Hebrew badim. Other pieces of the sanctuary have poles too, but for the ark the Torah says it outright: they stay in. Always. The Talmud treats this as a real commandment: pulling the poles out of the ark would break a prohibition. Why? The Torah doesn't say. Some said it was so no one would need to handle the holy ark directly when it moved. Others read a message in it. Rabbi Samson Raphael Hirsch, a German commentator, wrote that the poles show the Torah inside was never meant to be tied to one place. Wherever the people go, it goes with them. Later, when Solomon set the ark in the Temple in Jerusalem, the book of Kings says the poles were still in, so long their ends could be seen from the holy place. Even at rest, it was ready to travel. Later Jewish readers found that detail fitting. In exile, Jews carried the Torah to Babylon, to Spain, to Poland, to Yemen, to New York. The ark was gone, but the habit of readiness stayed. And with that, Terumah ends: willing hearts, among them, gold inside and out, the facing cherubim, and the poles that stay in.
screen: `THE STAVES SHALL BE IN THE RINGS.` · `THE TALMUD: NEVER REMOVE THEM.` · `HIRSCH: NOT TIED TO ONE PLACE.` · `STILL IN, EVEN IN THE TEMPLE.` · then, large: `READY TO TRAVEL.`

segments.voice: Suppose you had to move tomorrow, somewhere far. Not the furniture: name one or two things that make you who you are, a habit, a few words you live by, a practice from this path, a voice you'd keep in your head. Then ask whether each is ready to travel, or only works in one room, one routine.
Terumah. The portion we finish today, whose ark keeps its carrying poles in, always ready to travel with its people.
Your line: ready to travel. A week of laws and gifts: the widow, do then understand, willing hearts, the inside gold, the facing faces. Until tomorrow.
